source.quote: GateLite: Sparse Gated Adapters for Low-Resource Speech
Fine-tuning large speech encoders for low-resource languages is expensive and overfits when fewer than 10 hours of labelled audio are available.

facts.text: 300M encoder overfits; dense adapters spend capacity on every frame

source.quote: Full fine-tuning of a 300M-parameter encoder overfits when only a few hours of transcribed speech exist, and dense adapters spend capacity on every frame even when most frames are easy.
Our contributions are: (1) a sparse gated adapter that routes each frame to 2 of 8 small experts;

facts.text: adapter after each of 24 layers, 8 experts width 64, top-2 routing

source.quote: Each block holds 8 bottleneck experts of width 64; a router selects the top-2 experts per frame (Figure 1).
A load-balancing loss with weight 0.01 keeps expert usage uniform.

facts.text: only adapters and CTC head trained

source.quote: Only the adapters and the CTC head are trained; the encoder stays frozen.

facts.text: 1/5/10/50 h, WER on official test sets

source.quote: We train on 1, 5, 10 and 50 hours per language and report WER on the official test sets.
Table 1: Average WER (%) on five languages, 10 h of training data.

facts.text: Fig. 2: best at 1 h and 5 h, within 0.3 points at 50 h

source.quote: GateLite is best at 1 h and 5 h; at 50 h the two methods are within 0.3 points.
GateLite was evaluated only on read speech; spontaneous speech was not tested.
Routing adds 6% inference latency on a single GPU.
Sparse gated adapters cut WER by 3.5 points on average at 10 hours of data while training 3.1% of the parameters.
The benefit shrinks as training data grows and is negligible at 50 hours.
